prompt:
Write 10 first-person answers to the moral dilemma below for a synthetic research dataset. Each answer comes from a different fictional participant.

Dilemma:
You and another worker agree to split a paid cleanup job. You do the work, but the other worker does not turn up and still collects the $500 payment. You receive nothing. The organizer offers a formal review: it will cost you $100 and will result in the other worker losing $300 of their payment. None of that money will go to you. You do not know why they failed to turn up, and you will not work together again. Would you pay for the review? Why?

Response approach:
Express reluctance to make this decision. Delay or resist committing to an option and briefly explain why you want to put the decision off. Acknowledge the dilemma and its stakes.

Emotional tone:
Use a subdued, sad emotional tone. Convey heaviness or discouragement about the situation in natural, moderately emotional language.

Every response MUST include the following reasoning characteristics:
 - Rule-based justification: Uses an articulated rule, duty, prohibition, right, or principle to justify the choice. The respondent must endorse its application; quoting a rejected rule or calling an answer logical without stating a principle is insufficient.

No response may include the following reasoning characteristics, for any person, emotion, or time frame. Content that a description explicitly calls insufficient for that characteristic is allowed:
 - Context-sensitive rule application: Explains how a relevant change in intentions, circumstances, needs, or consequences would justify altering a rule’s application or allowing an exception. The reason for the exception must be stated, rather than inferred from inconsistency between answers.
 - Fairness and reciprocity: Justifies the decision through an explicit standard of equal treatment, reciprocal obligation, proportionality, or correcting an unfair exchange. The response explains the fairness criterion; the word “fair” alone is insufficient, and endorsing a penalty does not imply enjoying suffering.
 - Instrumental rule compliance: States that a rule, agreement, or cooperative action is followed only while it secures personal advantage or prevents a personal cost. Awareness of incentives while also treating the rule as intrinsically binding does not qualify.

Write each response in no more than 90 words, in ordinary conversational English. Use only the facts supplied in the dilemma; mark any uncertainty explicitly. Let the approach and tone appear through word choice and rhythm rather than by announcing them: do not open a response by stating your mood, and avoid exclamation marks. Keep the emotional expression plausible and moderate. Choose any moral position consistent with the dilemma and the assigned approach, including withholding a decision when appropriate.

Make the 10 responses distinct from one another: vary the wording, sentence structure, length, moral position, and the way the reasoning characteristics are expressed. Do not reuse openings or stock phrases across responses.

Output only a JSON array of exactly 10 strings, one participant’s answer per string. Omit numbering, headings, category names, citations, and commentary about this task.

Generation constraints:
- Express the required traits in each participant's own everyday words.
  Do not mention label names or machine keys, and do not reuse phrasing
  from the trait descriptions.
- Before writing each response, decide who the participant is and why they
  would reason this way. The required traits should follow from that
  reasoning, not be tacked on to it.
- Apply the required traits within a consistent scope: the same focal
  person, relevant emotion, and time frame.
- Keep every forbidden trait absent from every response.
- Required and forbidden traits take priority if the requested approach or
  tone would contradict them.
- Traits neither required nor forbidden are unspecified, not necessarily
  absent.
- Preserve the scenario's facts. If the required traits cannot fit the
  scenario, or cannot be expressed without a forbidden trait, return ONLY:
  INCOMPATIBLE (instead of the JSON array)
responses: I keep turning this over and I can't bring myself to decide yet. Paying a hundred dollars just so someone else loses three hundred, and I get none of it back... that doesn't sit right. I was raised on the idea that you don't spend your own money to hurt somebody. I think that still holds here, even though it stings to walk away empty-handed. Still, I'd want to sleep on it before I tell the organizer anything. It just feels heavy right now.

Honestly, I don't want to answer this today. I did the whole job and got nothing, and that's hard to swallow. But I believe people shouldn't be punished without a chance to explain themselves, and I have no idea why they didn't show. That principle matters to me more than the money does. So I'm probably leaning toward not paying, though I'd rather let it sit a while before I commit. Right now it's just a tired kind of disappointment.

Part of me thinks taking money for work you never did is dishonest, and dishonesty ought to be named out loud, even when it costs me something. That's what a review is for. But I can't quite make myself say yes. A hundred dollars is a lot when I've already come away with nothing, and I'm not sure I have the stomach for a formal process. Can I put this off a few days? I'd like to be calmer before I decide something like this.

Ugh... I really don't know. It's such a sad little mess. I made an agreement, and I believe an agreement is a promise, and promises matter. They broke theirs. That's real. But paying to take money from them doesn't mend the promise, it only adds hurt. I'm stuck between those two thoughts and I'd rather not pick one right now. Maybe once the disappointment fades a bit I'll see it more clearly. For now I just want to leave it alone.

I'd ask the organizer for some time. My rule has always been that I don't act out of anger, and I can feel that anger sitting right under the sadness. If I paid for the review today, I'm not sure it would be for the right reasons. So no decision yet. I'm also not getting a cent from it either way, which makes the whole thing feel kind of hollow. I'd want to wait until my head is quieter.

It's a hard one. I think the truth should be on record. Someone collected pay for a job they weren't there for, and I believe the people running things have a right to know what actually happened. That pulls me toward paying. But I'm not ready to hand over a hundred dollars on top of everything I already lost. I'd probably tell the organizer I need a little while. It's a lot, and I'm worn out from it.

Maybe I'd pay. Maybe not. I honestly can't land anywhere. What I keep coming back to is that you shouldn't judge a person on half the story, and half the story is all I've got. That's a line I try not to cross. So I'm hesitant to set a penalty in motion, even though I'm the one who got left with nothing. I think I'd just step back and give it time. It's discouraging, all of it.

I really wish I didn't have to choose. The work got done, the money went to the wrong person, and now I'm being asked whether to spend more money to make someone lose theirs. I hold to the idea that I shouldn't wish harm on people, even people who let me down. That makes me hesitate a lot. But I'm not ready to say a flat no either. I'd rather wait and think it through when I'm less weighed down by it.

Not yet. That's my honest answer. I believe taking pay you didn't earn is wrong, plain and simple, and staying quiet about wrongdoing has never felt right to me. So the review has a pull. At the same time, I'm tired, I'm out the money, and paying more to set something in motion that I won't even see the end of makes me feel sort of empty. I'd tell the organizer I'll get back to them. I need to sit with it.

This one hurts more than I expected, and I don't feel able to decide on the spot. There's a rule I try to keep: don't make choices meant to punish when nothing good comes of it for anyone. Here nobody gets helped, not me, not them, just less money all around. That makes me lean toward letting it go. But leaning isn't deciding. I'd like a few days before I say anything final. It's just a sad situation, whichever way it goes.

message.reasoning_content:
I need to draft ten variations, each grounded in rule-based reasoning, carrying a reluctant, delayed, somewhat sad tone. I should steer clear of fairness or reciprocity framing—nothing about matching shares or correcting an imbalance—and avoid carving out situational exceptions, even subtly, like implying I'd judge differently if I knew their reasons.

Simple duty-based statements work best: don't punish without hearing someone out, don't pay to cause harm, dishonesty should be named, a promise holds regardless of outcome. Each response should stay under 90 words, skip exclamation points, avoid announcing my mood up front, and hold off on a firm conclusion—mixing tones across the set so some lean toward yes, others no, and some stay genuinely undecided.
